about: External figures and labelled assumptions quoted on docs/index.html and docs/pitch/. Each external figure lists its source and the date it was read; an assumption is marked as one and is never a measurement.

external.claim: Tower controllers detect 63 % of pilots' read-back errors and radar approach controllers 50 %, as cited from the literature.
external.source: Helmke et al., Readback Error Detection by Automatic Speech Recognition to Increase ATM Safety, ATM Seminar 2021

external.claim: Automatic read-back error detection (ASR + understanding) in controller trials of the HAAWAII project.
external.source: Helmke et al., Readback Error Detection by ASRU, Results of HAAWAII Project for Isavia's Enroute Airspace, SESAR Innovation Days 2022

external.claim: Goodyear, Houston, 2008: an isolation valve on the relief path was left closed after maintenance and the remaining relief path was then blocked.
external.source: US Chemical Safety Board, Goodyear case study, section 4.2

external.claim: Palm-oil mills in operation in Indonesia in 2022.
external.source: Trase, SEI-PCS Indonesia palm oil methodology v1.2.2 (Sept 2024)

external.claim: PP 50/2012 Article 5: every company with at least 100 workers or a high hazard potential must implement SMK3, which is audited.
Indonesia's personal data protection law (UU PDP), enacted 17 October 2022; voice that identifies a person is personal data.
The read-back check is the human-performance tool called three-way communication.
external.source: US DOE, DOE-HDBK-1028-2009 Human Performance Improvement Handbook, Vol. 2
external.note: named in the project spec; no URL recorded here

assumptions.assumption: 30 % of the operating mills are addressable: group-owned and dispatching isolation work by radio.
6 radio channels per palm-oil mill: control room, boiler and power house, press, maintenance, loading, security.
USD 2,400 per monitored channel per year (USD 200 a month), an on-prem licence.
1,318 x 30 % x 6 channels x USD 2,400 = about USD 5.7 M a year: the mills line only, the floor of the Indonesian beachhead.
